title: Efficient Reinforcement Learning – Rhythm Garg & Linden Li, Applied Compute
talk_summary: Applied Compute describes how they make RL training runs fast, cheap, and low-variance by moving from synchronous to asynchronous pipeline RL, then modeling the GPU allocation between sampling and training to maximize throughput under a staleness constraint. The transferable core is the systems-modeling method: fit empirical latency/throughput curves, simulate configurations before running, and prune by hard constraints.

takeaways.technique: Simulate scheduling configs before running them
takeaways.what_they_do: They build a first-principles model of the end-to-end system (per-GPU latency curve, training throughput, response-length distribution) and sweep configurations in simulation, pruning any that violate constraints, instead of paying for real runs to find the best layout.
takeaways.numbers: ~60% speedup vs synchronous baseline in simulation

takeaways.technique: Break lockstep to kill straggler idle time
takeaways.what_they_do: Synchronous RL waits for the slowest sample, leaving workers idle; they decouple sampling from training so workers never stop, accepting bounded staleness in exchange for utilization.
takeaways.evidence_quote: 99% of the samples completed in about 40 seconds, took another 80 seconds to get that last percent

takeaways.what_they_do: They formalize an invariant that sampling (production) and training (consumption) throughput must be roughly equal; too many producers causes unbounded staleness, too many consumers causes idle workers.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the production and consumption rate are roughly equal

takeaways.what_they_do: They cap how stale a sample can be (how many policy updates behind) and prune configs exceeding it, trading throughput against learning quality.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we want a lot of staleness for faster RL runs, but a lot of staleness makes learning unstable

takeaways.technique: Fit empirical latency curves, not guesses
takeaways.what_they_do: They fit a latency-vs-batch-size curve (memory-bound then compute-bound, roofline-based) and a per-GPU training throughput curve from real workloads, then use those as model inputs.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we can fit a latency curve as a function of batch size
